intro: Every person starts life in a particular place, a particular family and a particular language. Some start with more money, some with less. Some grow up speaking the language of their grandparents, and some grow up between two languages. This unit looks at the world today and asks how much those starting points shape a life, and how people move beyond them.

In the first chapter you will learn how economists measure gaps between rich and poor, and how easily children move up or down compared with their parents. You will compare Norway, Brazil, Britain, India and China. In the second chapter you will follow music, food and people across borders. You will study how countries welcome newcomers and how communities keep languages alive. Then you will walk through four Chicago neighborhoods.

By the end, you will be able to read a Gini score and a mobility chart and explain what they show. You will be able to describe the main views on inequality and migration fairly. You will also be able to use evidence to argue your own answer to the unit's big question.
bigQuestion: How much do birth, class and culture shape who we become, and how do people and societies change them?

test.q: Which is an example of wealth?
choices: Savings and a house, minus debts
test.why: Wealth is what you own minus what you owe; the others are forms of income.

test.q: A Gini coefficient of 0 would mean:
choices: One person has all the income
test.why: A Gini of 0 means perfect equality; a Gini of 1 means one person has everything.

test.q: Which region is often described as one of the most unequal in the world?
test.why: Latin American countries such as Brazil and Colombia have some of the highest Gini scores.

choices: Children's position with their parents' position
test.why: Intergenerational mobility measures how children's position differs from their parents'.

test.q: Why is the Great Gatsby curve called a correlation?
choices: It proves inequality causes low mobility
It shows two measures moving together without proving cause
test.why: A correlation shows a pattern; other differences between countries could help explain it.

test.q: In Britain, schools like Eton are called:
test.why: In Britain, old fee-paying private schools are confusingly called public schools.

test.q: Who led the committee that wrote India's Constitution?
test.why: Ambedkar, born into a caste treated as untouchable, led the drafting committee.

test.q: What helped close to 800 million people in China leave extreme poverty?
test.why: The World Bank links China's huge drop in extreme poverty to growth after the 1978 reforms.

test.q: Which explanation of inequality is most often stressed on the political right?
test.why: The right often stresses freedom, markets and personal responsibility; the left often stresses structural causes.

test.q: Which is an example of cultural hybridity?
choices: A language with no new words
Reggaeton mixing reggae, hip-hop and Latin rhythms
test.why: Hybridity is mixing traditions into something new, as reggaeton does.

test.q: Money that migrants send to family in their home country is called:
test.why: Remittances are a major source of income for countries such as Mexico and the Philippines.

test.q: Which country adopted multiculturalism as official policy in 1971?
test.why: Canada was one of the first countries to make multiculturalism official policy.

test.q: An endangered language is one that:
choices: Children are no longer learning at home
test.why: When children stop learning a language at home, it is at risk of disappearing.

test.q: Which Chicago street is known for South Asian shops alongside a long-standing Jewish community?
test.why: Devon Avenue in West Ridge is known for its Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi businesses and its Jewish community.

test.q: Rising rents that push longtime residents out of Pilsen are an example of:
test.why: Gentrification is when wealthier newcomers move in and costs rise.

write.prompt: Does the place and family a person is born into matter more today than a person's own choices? Take a position. Use two or three facts or sources from the unit, such as the Gini data, the Great Gatsby curve, Chetty's research, China's reforms or a Chicago neighborhood, and explain how they support your claim.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence at the start.
Name each source or measure you use, such as the World Bank or the Sutton Trust.
Describe the strongest view that disagrees with you, fairly.
Use unit terms like social mobility, wealth and assimilation correctly.
End by explaining what your evidence can and cannot prove.
